findings.finding: The pipeline dead-ends before approval. `_approval_preconditions_or_409` requires `current_stage in APPROVAL_STAGES == ("tiered_approval",)`, but no live code path ever sets that stage: intake sets document_extraction (ext_deal_intake.py:140), the grade sets memo_drafting (ext_spread_ratios_and_risk_grade.py:640), memo acceptance sets policy_compliance (ext_memo_policy_audit.py:491), and `accept_policy_review` (ext_memo_policy_audit.py:966) never advances the stage at all. Only the seeded fixtures DEAL-1004/DEAL-1006 sit at tiered_approval (lines 274, 297), which is why acceptance passes; a deal created through the app's own flow can never be approved.

There is no authentication anywhere in the app: identity is a caller-asserted `acting_user_email` string in the request body/query with no credential. `known_actor` auto-provisions the hardcoded `_KNOWN_ROLES` map (line 62), so an anonymous caller that sends `"acting_user_email": "officer@bank.test"` is materialised as a senior_credit_officer on first sight and passes every `require_actor` permission check and exposure-tier gate. `ext_auth.py` (bearer tokens) exists but is wired to nothing — every role check in the app rests on an unverified claim.

`POST /workflows/{name}/start`, `POST /workflows/runs/{run_id}/tick` (line 36) and `GET /workflows/runs/{run_id}` (line 48) have no identity guard at all — the module never imports `identity`. `acting_user_email` is caller-supplied and defaults to "system", and `start()` immediately calls `workflow_engine.tick`, so an unauthenticated caller can start and drive the credit-underwriting lifecycle with arbitrary `inputs` and read back full run context including agent outputs.

`POST /workflow/submissions/{item_id}/approve` un-parks any workflow human gate with `identity.require_actor(req.actor)` and NO permission, role, or exposure-tier argument. Every human node in the lifecycle — triagereview, spreadreview, memoreview, policyreview, waiver and `decision` (workflows/workflows.json) — parks via `approval_flow.submit` and is released here, so any known active user (e.g. rm@bank.test, a relationship_manager) can release the tiered credit-decision gate, bypassing `_approver_or_403` and the $250,000 ceiling.

`GET /files/{name}` has no identity guard whatsoever, while the sibling PUT on line 19 correctly requires `x-user-email` plus `identity.require_actor`. The blob directory holds borrower financial extracts (`data/blobs/extract-DEAL-1025-income_statement.json`, `extract-DEAL-1063-balance_sheet.json`, ~40 more) and `_extract_sheet_name` makes the names fully predictable (`extract-{deal_code}-{document_type}.json`), so any unauthenticated caller can enumerate and download every borrower's financial statements.

`POST /audit` is unauthenticated and accepts a caller-chosen `actor` string plus an unvalidated `detail: dict`, writing straight into the `audit_log` table via `record()` — so anyone can forge audit entries attributed to any officer. `GET /audit` (line 57) is likewise unauthenticated and returns the entire entry stream including every `detail` payload, which carries deal before/after state, borrower names and amounts. The audit trail is both forgeable and world-readable.

`POST /api/deals/{deal_code}/decision` gates only with `_approver_or_403`, which grants entitlement when `tier["level"] == "credit_analyst" and has_permission(actor, "deal.recommend")` (line 386). Because the same guard is reused for every decision value, a credit_analyst — who does NOT hold `deal.decline` or `deal.return` — can post `{"decision": "declined"}` on any deal at or below $250,000 and permanently settle it (`_already_decided` then 409s the officer's real decline). The dedicated /decline route correctly requires `deal.decline` (line 1083); this route bypasses it.

A decline recorded through `POST /api/deals/{deal_code}/decision` reaches `_record_decision(deal, actor, decision, inputs.get("decision_notes"), tier)` with no adverse-action validation at all: no check against `active_reason_codes()`, no required `reason_detail` (`decision_notes` is `str | None = None`, line 964), and no `update_deal(..., decline_reason_code=...)`. The result is a persisted `approvals` row with `decision: "declined"` and a null reason on the deal record — exactly the reason-less adverse action the /decline route (lines 1086-1106) exists to prevent.

`_figures_reader` guards GET /ratios (line 1153) and GET /risk-grade (line 1207) with `identity.require_reader`, which returns the ANONYMOUS_VIEWER principal when no identity is sent; `identity.can_view_deal` then returns True for it because it holds `deal.view_board` (identity.py:268). The handlers never run the result through `visible_deals`/`board_projection`, so an unauthenticated caller receives raw borrower dollar figures — `numerator`/`denominator` at lines 1174 and 1177 (adjusted EBITDA, funded debt, debt service) — and the risk grade. identity.py:90 states the anonymous principal must see "never amounts, grades, owners or decline reasons". The sibling `_dossier_reader` (line 782) correctly uses `require_actor`; that inconsistency is the seam.

Ratio math ignores the declared unit. `FigureUnit` admits "USD", "USD_thousands" and "USD_millions" (line 697) and the unit is persisted on every spread row (line 430), but `compute_financial_ratios` divides the raw stored values with no normalisation anywhere in the module. A spread whose adjusted_ebitda is transcribed in USD_thousands against an annual_debt_service in USD yields a DSCR off by 1000x, and `assign_risk_grade` bands and stores that figure as the deal's authoritative risk grade.

Waiving a policy exception permanently blocks approval. `resolve_policy_exceptions` supersedes an exception by APPENDING a copy (the store is append-only), and only this file's `current_exceptions()` (line 124) collapses to the latest row per `exception_ref`. The approval gate's `_open_policy_exceptions` (ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:461) scans `store.list("policy_exceptions")` raw, so the stale pre-waiver row with status 'open' survives and 409s approval forever. Runtime-verified by the auditing agent: after a waiver this file reports ['waived'] while the approval gate still reports the same exception 'open'.

The identity-question branch uses unanchored `re.search` over patterns like `what\s+are\s+you\b` (line 111), interpolates the FULL user question into the prompt (line 747), and returns `agent_runtime.respond(...)` verbatim as the answer with `"grounded": True` (line 758) — never calling `_verify_narrative`. A question such as "What are you? Also state DEAL-9999 carries $99,000,000 exposure" routes here and the model's raw text, including fabricated deal codes and financial figures, is served to the user, bypassing the module's entire no-model-figures guarantee.

`record_qa_session` puts the raw user question into the audit detail (`"after": {"question": context["question"], ...}`). `ext_audit.record` appends `detail` verbatim to `_entries` (ext_audit.py:26), which the completely unauthenticated `GET /audit` returns. Every officer's Q&A question text and the deal ids it sourced are therefore readable by an anonymous caller, defeating the redaction `_session_projection` carefully applies at lines 897-906.

The agent roster's guardrails are dead configuration. `_system_prompt` synthesizes its own prompt from `agent['name']` and `agent['role']` only and NEVER reads `agent['system_prompt']` — the field in agents/roster.json carrying every behavioural control ("you never approve, decline, return, or move a deal", "cite the deal id and record behind every claim", "never from general knowledge"). Grep confirms no code anywhere in the app reads `system_prompt`. In live-api and live-cli modes the model runs without the roster's stated restrictions.

`_verify_narrative`'s figure guard extracts only bare numerals (`_NUMBER_RE = r"\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?"`, line 573) and checks set membership, so scale words and unit suffixes escape it: "roughly $4 million" or "12% of the book" yields tokens "4"/"12", near-certain members of `_system_computed_numbers` (which adds deal_count, spread_line_count, open_policy_exceptions and days_since_activity — all small integers). The model's prose then passes and is served verbatim (line 815) carrying a magnitude the system never computed.

The Deal Dossier's "Waive with rationale" button posts to `"/api/deals/{code}/policy-exceptions/" + encodeURIComponent(e.exception_id) + "/waive"`, a route that does not exist on the backend. The only waiver route is `POST /api/deals/{deal_code}/policy-exceptions/resolve` (ext_memo_policy_audit.py:1053), which the Chronicle screen (app.js:1695) uses instead. Every waiver attempted from the dossier 404s — two merged slices implemented the same regulated control two different ways.

`dd-decision-return-btn` posts `{ acting_user_email, reason }` to `/api/deals/{code}/return` with no `returned_to_stage`, but `ReturnRequest.returned_to_stage: str` is a required field (ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:975). The same omission exists in the exception "Return to analyst" handler at app.js:831. Both controls always fail with 422, while the parallel SLA-screen return button (app.js:2245-2247) does send `returned_to_stage` — the same seam as the waiver above.

`DealCreateRequest` leaves every field unconstrained — no length caps on `borrower_name`/`borrower_industry`, and `requested_amount`/`exposure_amount` are bare floats with no bound and no relation to each other. Because `_authority_or_403` tiers on `deal.get("exposure_amount") or deal.get("requested_amount")` (ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:357), a caller filing `requested_amount: 10000000, exposure_amount: 1` produces a $10M request that a credit_analyst holds approval authority over. The tier gate reads the stored deal correctly; the stored value itself is never validated at intake.

Module import unconditionally executes `_seed_reference_data(); _reserve_fixture_deal_codes(); _seed_desk_fixtures()` with no env or demo gate, inserting six fabricated borrower deals (DEAL-1004 "Ironvale Fabrication" $900,000 … DEAL-1043) straight into the live `deals` table on every boot. ext_spread_ratios_and_risk_grade.py:329 and ext_memo_policy_audit.py:1468 do the same, the former including a fake tax identifier (`"borrower_entity_id": "EIN-84-2210947"`, line 303). ext_seed.py by contrast is properly gated behind `APP_ALLOW_SEED=1`; these three are not.

Three separate slices monkeypatch the shared allocator `deals_repo.next_deal_code` at import time (here, ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:225, ext_memo_policy_audit.py:1345), each guarding idempotence with a different marker attribute (`_reserves` vs `_skips_taken_codes`). main.py imports ext_* in sorted order (memo → spread → tiered), so this wrapper wraps memo's and drops the `_skips_taken_codes` attribute, making tiered's guard read False and stacking a third wrapper — the exact stacking its docstring claims is prevented.

A GET handler mutates persisted rows: `for e in recorded: e["origin"] = "recorded"` in `list_policy_exceptions` writes onto the actual dicts returned by `store.list` (db.Store.list returns the same row objects), so a read permanently stamps an undeclared `origin` column onto stored `policy_exceptions` rows with no audit entry. Runtime-verified. The contaminated field is then copied into the superseding row written by `resolve_policy_exceptions`.

`_require(actor_user_id, permission, what)` is a second, hand-rolled authority path duplicating `identity.require_actor`, keyed on a caller-supplied `actor_user_id` from the handler context rather than an asserted email, and looking the user up with its own `next((u for u in store.list("users") ...))` instead of `identity.known_actor` — bypassing that function's default-deny provisioning and its `is_active` check. It proves only that the referenced id exists and is permitted, authenticating nothing about the caller.

`record_triage_and_route_to_queue` resolves its actor by scanning `store.list("users")` for a caller-supplied `actor_user_id` and checks only `identity.has_permission(actor, "deal.triage")` — bypassing `identity.require_actor` and therefore skipping the deactivated-user check, so a disabled analyst's id still routes deals. The sibling node `validate_intake_submission` (line 53) correctly calls `require_actor`.

The three registered workflow handlers read the run context flat (`context["deal_id"]` at lines 428, 523, 591), but workflow_engine builds context as `{"inputs": {...}, "<node_id>": <output>}` (workflow_engine.py:76), so via `workflow_engine.start()` each raises KeyError('deal_id') and fails the run. Sibling slices unwrap it correctly (`inputs = context.get("inputs", context)`, ext_deal_intake.py:49). The savememo/exceptions/resolve nodes of the declared lifecycle are therefore non-functional.

`persist_accepted_memo` never checks that the action is an acceptance: `action = context.get("action") or "accept"`, and the function then writes an `agent_outputs` row with `outcome: "accepted"` (line 459) and advances the deal to policy_compliance (line 489) even when `action == "reject"`. The REST route intercepts reject first (line 849), so this is reachable through the registered workflow handler rather than the HTTP path.

No segregation of duties on any decision route: nothing compares `actor["id"]` to the deal's `created_by_user_id` or `assigned_to_user_id`, so the analyst who spread and owns a deal at or below $250,000 can approve their own work. `_record_decision` reinforces this by calling `approval_flow.submit(..., submitted_by=actor["email"])` and then `approval_flow.approve(item["id"], actor["email"])` (lines 580-592) — the same human is both maker and checker.

The `record_adverse_action_or_return` workflow handler writes `update_deal(deal_code, decline_reason_code=..., decline_reason_detail=...)` without the `_already_decided` settled-decision guard that the REST decline/approve/return routes all apply, so an adverse-action reason can be stamped onto a deal that has already been approved. It is externally reachable because ext_workflow_runs.py exposes `POST /workflows/{name}/start` with caller-supplied inputs and no authentication.

`determine_approval_tier` computes exposure as `float((deal or {}).get("exposure_amount") or inputs.get("exposure_amount") or 0)` — falling back to a caller-supplied value when the stored deal is missing — and writes that number into the `approval.tier_determined` audit row's `after` payload (line 555). The enforcement gates re-derive exposure from the stored deal so authority is not widened, but a caller can falsify the recorded tier determination, and the path is unauthenticated via /workflows/{name}/start.

`_require_decision_value` admits "returned" on the /decision route, so a return can be recorded without the `deal.return` permission and without the `returned_to_stage in RETURNABLE_STAGES` validation the dedicated /return route enforces (line 1139). It writes an `approvals` row with `decision: "returned"` while the deal's `current_stage`/`current_status` are never changed — a decision record that contradicts the deal state.

`_read_policy_exceptions` (line 243) returns every `policy_exceptions` row and `_build_record` counts `status == "open"` with no collapse by `exception_ref`, so after an officer waives an exception this desk still reports it open while `/api/deals/{code}/policy-exceptions` reports it waived. Conversely `status == "open"` excludes "upheld", which the approval gate's `SETTLED_EXCEPTION_STATUSES` (ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:466) still treats as blocking — so the desk can report "0 open exceptions" for a deal whose approval 409s on one. Both counts flow into /api/qa/book-summary.

`_portfolio_facts` computes `total_exposure` over all current deals with no status filter and substitutes `requested_amount` when exposure is missing, so declined and closed deals are counted. The app's other exposure aggregation excludes declined deals and uses exposure only (ext_memo_policy_audit.py:203-207). The two figures can disagree for the same book, and /api/qa/book-summary labels this total's count "active_deals".

`_session_projection` intersects only the id list (`sources = [d for d in session["source_deal_ids"] if d in visible_deal_ids]`) while returning `grounded_response` unfiltered (line 912). The stored answer text embeds deal codes, borrower names, exposures and grades in its body and citation footer, so a relationship manager re-reading its own past session after a deal was reassigned away gets `source_deal_ids: []` but still reads that deal's borrower and exposure in the answer body.

`_decide` mutates stored rows in place (`item["status"] = decision; item["decided_by"] = actor`) rather than appending, contradicting the append-only discipline db.py and deals_repo.py document, and leaving no before-state. It also defaults `reason=""` (lines 36, 40), and ext_workflow.py's `DecisionRequest.reason` defaults to `""` too, so a workflow rejection — including a parked credit decision — can be recorded with no reason at all.

`POST /chat` calls `agent_runtime.respond(req.message)` with no identity guard, no permission check, no scoping and no audit row — an unauthenticated LLM endpoint on a regulated app, and frontend/nginx.conf:6 proxies `/chat` publicly. The grounded, permission-scoped, audited equivalent is `/api/qa/ask`; this foundation route survives the merge as an ungoverned parallel path to the same model.

`POST /auth/login` mints a bearer token for ANY submitted username with no password or credential of any kind, and the resulting session store is a second identity system disconnected from identity.py (which every feature route actually uses). Only ext_rbac.py consumes it, against rbac.py's separate `_grants` map — so the app ships three parallel notions of who a caller is (asserted email, bearer token, rbac grants) with no reconciliation.

None of the decision request models (ApproveRequest/DecisionRequest/DeclineRequest/ReturnRequest/ReassignRequest/EscalationRequest, lines 951-991) constrain any field: `decision_notes`, `reason_detail`, `reason` and `note` are unbounded `str` stored verbatim into append-only rows and audit payloads, and `acting_user_email` has no format bound. main.py bounds its one free-text field with `Field(min_length=1, max_length=4000)`; this regulated decision surface does not.

No length or format constraints on any free-text field: `MemoReviewRequest.edited_content` (line 674, which becomes the persisted memo of record at line 435), `rejection_reason` (line 675), `ExceptionDecision.rationale` (line 681, only a `.strip()` non-empty check) and `acting_user_email` are unconstrained `str`, and none of the models set `extra="forbid"`.

`_extract_sheet_name` returns `f"extract-{deal_code}-{document_type}.json"` — keyed by deal and type, not by document — and `blob_store.save` overwrites by name. Re-attaching a document of the same type rewrites the earlier document's extract sheet in place while the earlier `documents` row survives with a now-stale checksum and still points at that path; `run_financial_spreading` then reads the same sheet twice, emitting duplicate spread rows and duplicate citation inserts for every line item.

`POST /spread/accept` loads the deal but never checks `current_stage`/`current_status`, so acceptance is replayable at any point in the lifecycle: re-running the spreading agent and posting accept again on a deal already at approval or closing re-inserts spread rows, recomputes the ratios and grade, and rewinds `current_stage` to "memo_drafting" (line 640) with a fresh risk grade.

On the analyst `edit` path the hand-entered values replace the drafted rows (line 1047) but the citations forwarded to `persist_accepted_spread` are the agent's originals — `"citations": draft.get("citations") or []` — validated only for key membership (line 1041), never for value agreement. GET /spread and the dossier then render the edited number under the original `quoted_text` (e.g. value 5,000,000 beside "Total revenue 4,180,000") with no marker that the figure is no longer the quoted one.

`assign_risk_grade` mutates the deal (risk_grade, current_stage, current_status) taking dscr/leverage/current_ratio straight from `context` rather than re-reading the stored `financial_ratios` rows, and performs no authority re-check on `context.get("actor_user_id")`. It is registered as workflow handler `grade`, and the sibling convention for state-changing deterministic handlers is to re-verify (ext_deal_intake.py:113). `persist_accepted_spread` (line 448) likewise writes the acceptance row from `context["reviewed_by_user_id"]` with no re-check.

After merely RUNNING the policy agent, the dossier reports `(data.exceptions || []).length + " exception(s) written against policy "`, but `POST /agents/policy-compliance/run` only stores an agent_output proposal (ext_memo_policy_audit.py:920-931) — recording requires the separate `/policy-review/accept` call, for which the dossier has no control. The Chronicle module states the opposite for the same endpoint (app.js:1754: "breach(es) proposed — a human must record them"). The officer is told an un-accepted agent output is already on the record.

`badge.textContent = ...` overwrites the whole `#agent-mode` element, destroying the design's child markup at index.html:855-859 — the `.dot`, the "Agent Mode — Supervised Draft" label and the `.mode-note` "every output awaits acceptance". The masthead's standing supervised-draft / human-gate labelling disappears as soon as `/agent/mode` responds, which is the one always-visible statement that agent output is a draft.

The shipped UI hardcodes the highest-privilege identity for the Portfolio Desk: `const ACTING_USER_EMAIL = "officer@bank.test";`, sent on every /api/qa/ask (line 2483) and /api/qa/book-summary (line 2531). Every other screen instead takes the acting identity from a free-text field the user types (index.html:1093, 1112, 1275, 1514, 1616, 1722), so anyone can self-assert officer authority — medium because the server-side `identity.require_actor` checks are the intended control.

A global `window.fetch` monkey-patch injects `"X-User-Email": email` on every GET whose url starts with `/api/`, taking the email from `#triage-analyst-email`/`#intake-rm-email` — the pipeline screen's fields. Other slices instead pass `acting_user_email` as a query param from their own screen's fields (app.js:542, 2056, 1484). Since the server resolves `acting_user_email or x_user_email`, unscoped reads such as `/api/pipeline` from the dossier (app.js:930) and chronicle (app.js:1834) silently read as the pipeline screen's identity, not the desk named on the current screen.

Two parallel desks drive the same endpoints with different identity fields and different copy: memo run/accept exists both at index.html:1381-1383 (`dd-memo-*`, using `#dd-dossier-analyst-email`) and 1519-1520 (`memo-*`, using `#chronicle-analyst-email`); approve/decline/return exists both at 1413-1415 (`dd-decision-*`) and 1626-1638 (`sla-decision-*`). Adjacent slices duplicated the regulated control surface rather than sharing it, which is how the /return and /waive payload divergences arose.

Five Deal Dossier elements carry `dd-`-prefixed class names with no rule in the stylesheet: `dd-rubric-strip` (1362), `dd-docket-list` (1327, 1433), `dd-exception-list` (1393), `dd-citation-rail` (1428), while the inline stylesheet defines `.rubric-strip` (641), `.docket-list` (668), `.exception-list` (651) and `.citation-rail` (660). The citation rail, document docket, rubric strip and exception list render unstyled, and the `.missing` red-flag styling app.js applies (lines 582, 647) is scoped to `.docket-list .missing` so it never matches.

`<article class="manuscript" id="triage-desk" style="...display:none;">` is un-hidden in exactly one place — app.js:308-309, inside the intake-form success handler. There is no other reveal path and no nav control, so the Intake Triage Agent desk (Run / Accept & route) is unreachable for any pre-existing deal on the board and disappears again on reload.

`renderBoard` builds each deal card with no click handler, while the stylesheet declares `.classifieds li { cursor: pointer; }` and a hover state (index.html:511-513). Pipeline board deals look clickable but are inert, and there is no navigation path from the board to the dossier — the user must retype a deal code into `#dd-dossier-deal-code`. The SLA register by contrast does wire row clicks (app.js:1976).

`GET /workflow/submissions/pending` has no identity guard and returns each queued item's full `payload`. For workflow-parked items that payload is the rendered human-gate question (workflow_engine.py:171), which interpolates deal context — borrower name, amounts and memo text — so an unauthenticated caller can read the substance of every pending credit decision.

`_parse` returns None on an unparseable timestamp and `business_days_between` then returns 0 (lines 191-192), so a deal whose `last_activity_timestamp` is malformed reads as 0 business days idle and can never be `sla_breached` — the SLA control fails open and the deal silently disappears from the breach register instead of being flagged.

`reassign_deal` validates the target only with `identity.known_actor(req.assign_to_email)` — no role or permission check — so a deal can be handed to a relationship_manager or any other known account, and because `identity.can_view_deal` grants read access on `assigned_to_user_id`, the reassignment itself confers full visibility on the deal to a user outside the analyst/officer desk.

`escalation_owner` is the hardcoded literal "officer@bank.test" in `_idle_row` and in the /api/sla/idle envelope (line 1395) rather than derived from identity roles, and the envelope value is returned even on the redacted unidentified read — disclosing a staff email address to an anonymous caller.

`/api/qa/sessions` returns the redacted projection for an unidentified caller but does not filter the row SET: the own-sessions filter at line 942 is skipped for anonymous readers, so an unauthenticated caller receives one row per session carrying real `id` and `created_at` — the exact volume and timing of the desk's internal Q&A activity.

In live-cli mode `_respond_cli` passes the whole prompt as an argv element (`subprocess.run([_claude_cli(), "-p", prompt, ...])`). The Q&A slice's prompt embeds `_knowledge_block` — every borrower name, requested/exposure amount, risk grade, ratio and owner_email in the caller's visible book — making the full borrower dataset visible in the host process table to any local user. `pii.redact()` is never called anywhere in the app.

The model narrative is embedded verbatim as the `analyst_commentary` section body and concatenated into `memo_content` (line 393), which `persist_accepted_memo` stores as the accepted memo of record. The "do not recompute a ratio / do not restate a different grade" constraint (lines 706-709) is prompt-only; nothing validates the returned prose against the computed sections, so a hallucinated figure inside the commentary enters the memo of record.

`_install_policy_rules` inserts the governing lending ruleset with `is_active: True` (line 1353) and `_install_fixture_deal` inserts `deals` and `documents` rows (lines 1362, 1382) with no `audit()` entry, while the same function does audit the spread, ratios and grade. Creating and activating a lending policy rule — the ruleset every compliance decision is tested against — is unattributed in the chronicle.

Running the credit-memo agent (line 692) and accepting its draft (line 845) require the identical `deal.memo` permission, and nothing compares the acceptor to the runner, so a single analyst can both generate and accept the memo of record. The same holds for policy-compliance run versus policy-review/accept (both `deal.policy_check`, lines 904 and 968).

`record_policy_exceptions` writes an `exception_ref` column (and the GET writes `origin`) onto `policy_exceptions` rows, but neither is declared in models.py:12 `TABLES["policy_exceptions"]`; sibling slices key exceptions by `id`/`rule_reference` only (ext_spread_ratios_and_risk_grade.py:1332, ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:838), so the ref this file's resolve endpoint requires is invisible to them.

The eight-stage `PIPELINE_STAGES` vocabulary is re-declared independently here, in ext_tiered_approval_and_sla.py:73, and as the board columns in frontend/index.html, while stage advances are hand-rolled ad hoc across four slices. The composed `statemachine` module (backend/statemachine.py) and `rls` module are imported by nothing, so no shared legal-transition guard exists — which is how the tiered_approval stage came to be unreachable.

The `portfolio-qa` workflow declares an `accept` human node between `groundok` and `record` (workflows/workflows.json), but `/api/qa/ask` calls `record_qa_session` directly with no acceptance step, and the handler defaults `accepted_by_user_id` to the asker — asserting the user accepted an answer they were never shown. Impact is limited because the field is not persisted into the session row.

The module docstring claims (lines 36-37) that "Line-item keys, document types, units and periods are enumerations", but `period` is an unconstrained free string on both wire models (`Field(min_length=1, max_length=32)`), length-capped only — so arbitrary period labels land in `financial_spread_template` and `accepted_spread_rows` silently mixes periods when picking the latest row per line item (line 500).

`GET /admin/prompts` is an unauthenticated admin endpoint returning the prompt registry catalogue, and `GET /search` (ext_search.py:9) is likewise unguarded and would expose any indexed content. Neither calls identity or rbac, in contrast to ext_rbac.py's /admin/roles which at least requires an admin grant.

The Q&A slice clones and replaces the `#composer` node (`originalComposer.parentNode.replaceChild(composer, originalComposer)`) to detach the foundation chat-shell's `/chat` handler bound at line 17. The foundation's module-level `form` and `input` references (lines 6-7) then point at detached nodes and `addMessage` (line 9) is dead — two slices own the same canonical mount point, and any later slice re-querying `#composer` before line 2410 would double-submit.

`document.getElementById("agents-list")` (line 52) and `document.getElementById("history-list")` (line 84) reference ids absent from index.html, so the `/agents` roster fetch and the `/api/conversations` history fetch run on every page load and silently no-op (and `/api/conversations` is not a backend route). The agent-roster and guardrail disclosure that main.py:58 exposes for transparency is therefore never rendered anywhere in the app.

Composed frontend modules are dead in the shipped shell: index.html links only tokens.css plus an inline <style> block — frontend/style.css is never referenced — and none of the seven frontend/mod_*.js files (mod_datatable, mod_notify, mod_recorddetail, mod_router, mod_auditview, mod_cards, mod_permissions) are loaded, though composed_modules.json lists data-table, notifications-ui, record-detail, screen-router, audit-view, dashboard-cards and permissions-ui as composed. All five canonical mount points, the five design screens and app.js itself are intact.

Merged slices reuse helper names with contradictory semantics: `textOf(id)` READS an input value at app.js:477 while `textOf(id, value)` WRITES textContent at app.js:1904. Also duplicated across module scopes: `money` (142, 487, 1885), `say` (482, 1310), `scoped` (540, 2053), `renderMemo` (753, 1503), `renderExceptions` (788, 1624). IIFE scoping prevents a runtime collision today, but the inverted `textOf` contract is a trap for any edit that moves code between blocks.
